From the end of the Kamakura period, longer and heavier swords came into fashion, and the fashion carried on into the next age. When the Warring States brought mass tactics with spears and guns, the craze cooled. Cooled, I say, not died: among warriors it never fully went away.

Consider Juurouzaemon Magara, a mighty general in Asakura service, said to have swung a great sword of seven shaku three sun. Over seven feet. That is not a weapon, that is a lamppost with a bad temper.

Why did the fashion begin? Theories are many; certainty is nil. One theory blames the Mongol invasions. The Yamato warriors found the Mongol warriors' hard armor too much to handle, so they demanded a blade strong enough to break it. Logic of the simplest kind: wall is hard, hammer must be big.

But a great sword without the strength to wield it is only luggage. And circumstances bind it also.

Ground, especially ground with many obstacles, does not suit it. By the theory, the book answer, Ichijou should now take to the air. But—

It follows the old tale of two tigers so absorbed in their quarrel that they tumbled off a mountain and, even then, went on tearing at each other's throats. A gritty sound came from the wound.
Still burning. The heat had not gone away.
